ui_inventory.name: Form1 — Dashboard, Navigation Shell & Statistics View
ui_inventory.platform: Windows desktop (WinForms), .NET Framework 4.8, single x86 EXE, manually installed per workstation — no web/HTTP surface
ui_inventory.technology: VB.NET WinForms; inline ADO.NET/OleDb SQL (ten COUNT(*) aggregate queries); hosts InsertForm/ViewForm/EditForm by reparenting them into Panel5 (TopLevel=False)
ui_inventory.notes: Largest and most structurally complex surface: 1,211-line Designer file, 77 controls (21 Labels, 20 Panels, 17 PictureBoxes). Simultaneously the application's startup form, its navigation shell, its child-form host, and its only reporting/statistics view — see structural-analysis.json coupling_indicators 'god-form' and recommended_decomposition_boundaries 'ui-shell-and-navigation'. The dashboard's 'Project Report' button is not an in-app report: it shells out via Process.Start to a hardcoded public GitHub URL for a PDF (Form1.vb:155-157); recorded here as a UI affordance, not a generated report. Evidence: Flat Design/Form1.vb:1, Flat Design/Form1.Designer.vb:1, structural-analysis.json modules[0].

ui_inventory.name: InsertForm — New Student Record Entry
ui_inventory.technology: VB.NET WinForms; parameterized INSERT via inline OleDb SQL
ui_inventory.notes: 24 controls across 10 data-entry fields (Roll No, First Name, Last Name, Father Name, Gender combo, Date of Birth picker, Mob No, Alt Mob No, Course combo, Session/YOA combo) plus Save/Cancel. Reparented into Form1.Panel5 by btnNew_Click. No field validation, no MaxLength on any TextBox, and the post-save refresh calls Form1.LoadData()/ViewForm.LoadData() through VB default-instance aliasing rather than the on-screen instances (structural-analysis.json coupling_indicators 'default-instance-aliasing') — a correctness defect, not an accessibility one, but it affects what a screen-reader user is told happened after Save. Evidence: Flat Design/InsertForm.vb:1, Flat Design/InsertForm.Designer.vb:1.

ui_inventory.name: EditForm — Existing Student Record Editor
ui_inventory.technology: VB.NET WinForms; parameterized SELECT-by-rollno and UPDATE via inline OleDb SQL
ui_inventory.notes: Near-identical 24-control layout to InsertForm (same 10 fields), reached only from ViewForm's Update button with a roll number constructor argument. The one form in the application with a non-default constructor, so it is exempt from the default-instance aliasing defect but ViewForm must special-case it. Evidence: Flat Design/EditForm.vb:1, Flat Design/EditForm.Designer.vb:1.

ui_inventory.name: ViewForm — Student Record Grid, Search & Delete
ui_inventory.technology: VB.NET WinForms DataGridView bound to an OleDbDataAdapter DataSet, AutoGenerateColumns=True; free-text search (string-concatenated SQL, the application's one SQL-injection point); parameterized DELETE
ui_inventory.notes: 12 controls: search textbox, Search button, the grid, Update and Delete buttons. Launches EditForm and reaches into Form1.Panel5.Controls directly to host it. Column headers are the raw database field names (RollNo, FName, LName, FatherName, MobNo, AltMobNo, Gender, Course, YOA, DOB) because AutoGenerateColumns=True with no explicit HeaderText — see accessibility_findings A11Y-002. Evidence: Flat Design/ViewForm.vb:1, Flat Design/ViewForm.Designer.vb:1.

personas.name: Student-Records Operator (sole user class — no role differentiation observed)
personas.estimated_headcount: Unknown — no CMDB export, org chart, or user-count figure was provided at onboarding (catalog.json open_questions records the same gap). The application's own README and project report frame it as a single-developer academic/portfolio project; if ever deployed operationally this persona could plausibly range from 1 to a small back-office team, but no authoritative source confirms real-world deployment scale, and this is explicitly NOT a measurement.
personas.evidence: No role or permission model exists anywhere in source. AuthenticationMode.Windows is declared (Flat Design/My Project/Application.Designer.vb:26; Application.myapp:8) but My.User is never read by any form — identity-landscape.json identity_models[0] confirms this and rates the application boundary 'below-AAL1'. There is no login form, no users/credentials table, and no role or audit column on the single 'students' table (structural-analysis.json database-schema-summary). All four human-facing screens are reachable by anyone who launches the EXE and expose unrestricted create/read/update/delete over all student PII (structural-analysis.json coupling_indicators 'unprotected-pii-in-source-control'; identity-landscape.json assurance_gaps[0] 'no-mfa', severity high). The README's feature list (Dashboard, Insert, View, Update, Delete) and all three screenshots show one undifferentiated operator performing every function; no second role, approval step, or screen restricted from any user was found anywhere in the tree.
personas.typical_workflow: Launch the EXE → Form1 loads and immediately runs ten COUNT(*) aggregate queries to populate the dashboard tiles (no login step precedes this) → operator uses the left navigation rail to open Insert (add a new student's 10 fields and Save), View (search/browse the full grid, Delete a row, or launch Edit for a specific roll number), or returns to Dashboard. No session concept, no workflow approval gate, and no step-up/re-authentication exists at any point (Flat Design/Form1.vb:15; identity-landscape.json assurance_gaps 'no-session-timeout', 'no-step-up').

accessibility_findings.composed_from: cross-cutting accessibility-checker skill, dispatched at Discovery stage per ux-accessibility-assessor Methodology §4. accessibility_findings.gate_decision_note: Driven by one critical finding (A11Y-001: zero AccessibleName/AccessibleDescription across all 137 controls in all four forms — the application's only non-visual access mechanism is entirely absent) plus two serious findings. Per the accessibility-audit.json schema's own invariant, a critical violation forces the fail verdict; this is a legacy-baseline measurement for modernization comparison, not a Validation-stage gate on shipped code. Because the checker's method was a manual source read rather than an automated DOM scan, confidence is lower than a normal axe-core run (which itself only catches ~30-40% of issues) — treat every finding below as a floor, not a ceiling, on the true violation count.
manual_review_required: Live screen-reader pass (NVDA/JAWS/Windows Narrator) against a compiled build once one can be produced — this source-only audit cannot verify actual runtime announcement behavior, especially given the duplicate-TabIndex and overlapping-panel issues (A11Y-004, A11Y-005) that could affect live focus/reading order in ways source inspection alone cannot confirm

Pixel-level contrast measurement of rendered colors once a build exists — A11Y-006's contrast finding on the theme-dependent SystemColors.ActiveCaption tile is qualitative only; no pixel-sampled or tool-measured ratio was produced

End-to-end keyboard-only interaction test to confirm whether the duplicate TabIndex values (A11Y-004) and the two overlapping duplicate dashboard panels (A11Y-005) produce an actual keyboard trap or merely an inefficient tab order
verified_non_issues: Most dashboard tile color/text combinations use fixed, light pastel ARGB backgrounds (e.g. FromArgb(192,255,255), FromArgb(255,192,192), FromArgb(255,255,192)) paired with black text, which the checker judged unlikely to fail 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum on their qualitative review of the screenshots — the one exception found (Panel6 'Male Students' tile and the ViewForm grid background, which use theme-dependent SystemColors.ActiveCaption instead) is flagged separately as A11Y-006.

findings.summary: A full read of all four Designer.vb files confirms zero AccessibleName and zero AccessibleDescription property assignments across all 137 controls in the application (corroborating the prior structural-analysis pass). For controls that render visible .Text (buttons, labels) Windows UI Automation generally falls back to Text for a name, which is usually adequate, but for controls without inherent text content — ComboBox, DateTimePicker, DataGridView, PictureBox, TextBox — there is no reliable programmatic name at all, since WinForms has no formal label-for association comparable to HTML; adjacency to a Label is only a heuristic some screen readers use, and it is undermined here by the duplicate-TabIndex and overlapping-panel issues documented in A11Y-004/A11Y-005. This is the only mechanism (keyboard + screen reader) a non-visual user has to operate the application at all, so its total absence is classified critical. Location evidence: Form1.Designer.vb:173-215; InsertForm.Designer.vb:85-331; EditForm.Designer.vb:53-330; ViewForm.Designer.vb:42-171.

DataGridView1 is bound directly to the raw 'students' table with AutoGenerateColumns=True and no explicit Columns/HeaderText configuration in either ViewForm.vb or ViewForm.Designer.vb, so the rendered column headers are the literal database field names — confirmed in the application screenshot as RollNo, FName, LName, FatherName, MobNo, AltMobNo, Gender, Course, YOA, DOB. Abbreviations like 'YOA' and 'FName'/'LName' are not expanded anywhere in code or markup, so a screen reader announces the raw DB token with no explanation. Location evidence: ViewForm.vb:14, 37-45, 47-58; ViewForm.Designer.vb:81-130.

The five 'Year Wise' dashboard tiles (1st–5th year) all carry the identical generic text caption "Year Students" (Label27/Label17/Label23/Label25/Label12); the only element that actually distinguishes which year a given tile represents is a decorative numeral graphic rendered in a different color per tile, and none of those PictureBoxes has an AccessibleName. A user who cannot perceive the image/color has no way to tell the five tiles apart. Location evidence: Form1.Designer.vb:442-454, 491-503, 689-701, 738-750, 787-799 (labels); 456-464, 505-513, 703-711, 752-760, 801-809 (paired numeral PictureBoxes).

In the left navigation rail of Form1, btnReport and btnView both declare TabIndex = 6, and btnNew and btnHome both declare TabIndex = 7. Duplicate TabIndex values make the keyboard focus order through the primary navigation ambiguous/implementation-defined, which is a focus-order defect for keyboard-only users. Location evidence: Form1.Designer.vb:167, 189, 211, 254.

Panel11 (duplicate 'IIMCA Students' tile) and Panel13 (duplicate 'BCA Students' tile) are nested inside Panel10 with Location offsets that resolve to absolute positions overlapping the real Panel9 ('MCA Students') tile and sitting at the edge of the visible dashboard area respectively — leftover duplicate controls that remain part of the form's control collection and tab order. A keyboard/screen-reader user tabbing through the dashboard can land on content that does not correspond to anything sensible at that point in the reading sequence. Location evidence: Form1.Designer.vb:528-537, 577-586.

Most dashboard tiles use fixed, very light pastel ARGB values paired with black text, which the checker judged unlikely to fail contrast. The 'Male Students' tile (Panel6) and the ViewForm DataGridView background are exceptions: they use the theme-dependent SystemColors.ActiveCaption instead of a fixed color, which renders as a noticeably darker steel-blue in the screenshot and — more importantly — varies by Windows theme/accent color and OS version, so its actual contrast against the hard-coded black text is not fixed or verifiable at design time; a different theme or Windows high-contrast mode could produce a combination that fails AA even where the screenshot's rendering happens to pass. No pixel-sampled ratio was measured; this is a qualitative, source-grounded flag, not a measured failure. Location evidence: Form1.Designer.vb:960, 989; ViewForm.Designer.vb:89.

No TextBox in InsertForm or EditForm has MaxLength set, and neither code-behind file performs field-specific input validation before submitting to the database — the only error surfaced is a single generic MsgBox tied to the raw exception message, not to the offending field. Assistive-technology users get no advance indication of expected input length/format and no way to associate a validation failure with a specific field. Location evidence: InsertForm.Designer.vb:131-158, 193-200, 213-220, 222-229, 275-282; EditForm.Designer.vb:105-112, 125-132, 166-173, 186-193, 249-256; InsertForm.vb:4-34; EditForm.vb:49-73.

No Button.Text in any of the four forms contains an ampersand ('&'), confirming the prior structural-analysis pass's finding that there are no keyboard-shortcut/access-key (mnemonic) annotations anywhere in the application. All buttons remain reachable via Tab, so this is not a blocking keyboard failure, but it removes the Alt+accelerator efficiency path that keyboard-only and some motor-impaired users rely on. Location evidence: Form1.Designer.vb:168, 190, 212, 233, 255; InsertForm.Designer.vb:303, 318; EditForm.Designer.vb:64, 79; ViewForm.Designer.vb:68, 143, 158.

Internal control Name values are overwhelmingly generic/auto-generated (Label1 through Label27, Button8, Panel1 through Panel20, PictureBox1 through PictureBox17), but in nearly every case the VISIBLE .Text caption actually rendered to a sighted user is descriptive, so 2.4.6 is largely satisfied at the visual layer. The generic internal names only become a user-facing problem in combination with A11Y-001: for controls that have no .Text at all, Windows UI Automation has no visible caption to fall back on and may expose the literal internal Name to a screen reader. Lower priority than A11Y-001. Location evidence: Form1.Designer.vb:97, 217; InsertForm.Designer.vb:49, 324-331; EditForm.Designer.vb:28, 84-92; ViewForm.Designer.vb:37, 162-171.

review_asks.title: We found exactly one undifferentiated user type for this application — can you confirm that's the real picture?
review_asks.why: If a real deployment actually has more than one role (e.g. a supervisor who approves deletes, or a read-only reporting user), the accessibility and adoption-baseline findings in this artifact — and everything Deployment later compares post-cutover usage against — would be built on an incomplete persona model.

confidence.rationale: High confidence that the SOURCE CODE enforces no role distinction (zero authentication, zero permission checks, one table with no role column — this is a direct, exhaustive read of all 13 source files). Only low-to-medium confidence that this reflects actual real-world usage, because there is no telemetry, no CMDB, and no stakeholder input: the single persona is an inference from the absence of any role-enforcement mechanism in code, not a measurement of who actually uses the application or how many of them there are.

review_asks.assessment: This application has no login, no role model, and no permission checks anywhere in its source. Every screen (dashboard, insert, view/search, edit, delete) is reachable by anyone who launches the executable, with full read/write/delete access to all student records including PII (name, father's name, two phone numbers, date of birth). Because of this, the persona catalogue in this artifact contains exactly one entry — 'Student-Records Operator (sole user class)' — with an unknown headcount. This is an INFERENCE FROM CODE STRUCTURE, not a measurement: there is no usage telemetry, no CMDB entry, and no org chart for this application, so we cannot independently confirm how many people use it, whether they are in fact one undifferentiated group, or whether this is even in active use anywhere. A reviewer confirming this persona is confirming an inference presented honestly as an inference, not a measured fact.
review_asks.reasoning: The identity-landscape-analyzer pass independently reached the same single-persona conclusion from the identity/auth angle (user_classes: ['local-workstation-operator'] for both of the application's identity models). The structural-analysis pass reached it from the module/access-control angle (no authentication mechanism found anywhere; coupling_indicators 'unprotected-pii-in-source-control'). This assessment corroborates both from the UX/workflow angle: the README's own feature list and all three screenshots show one person doing everything. No conflicting signal was found anywhere, but the absence of a signal for a second persona is not proof that none exists in whatever real-world context this application runs in — the governing-profile mismatch (scope_caveat) means we also don't actually know what that real-world context is.
